title: Toward unity
hook: Catholics and Orthodox continue dialogue and marked 1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascha: a dark church, one flame, and a greeting shouted back at the doors. Your line was truly he is risen. Whose good news did you say back to them? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

Two old men in long robes walk toward each other in Jerusalem. One is the bishop of Rome. The other is the patriarch of Constantinople. Their churches have been divided for a long time, with excommunications on the books, hurt on both sides, and a long habit of not speaking. They don't sign a treaty. They don't settle a single doctrine. They embrace. Then they exchange a kiss of peace, the way the liturgy does it. A small gesture. Afterward, the old excommunications are lifted, and the two churches begin talking in earnest. Today, at the end of our days with the Eastern churches, the long road those two men started walking.
screen: `TWO OLD MEN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO TREATY. AN EMBRACE.` → `THE OLD EXCOMMUNICATIONS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Underneath it all is a prayer. At the supper before his arrest, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims, "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." The Catholic Church takes that prayer as a task, not a wish. Next, what Catholics and Orthodox already share, which is a great deal: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, the Creed of Nicaea, the early councils, the Mother of God, the saints, the icons. Catholics and Orthodox have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together, remembering a creed they both still pray. What divides them is real too, above all the role of the bishop of Rome, and it is worked on slowly, in official dialogue, by theologians from both sides. Then the honest part, about the churches we've spent these past days with. Eastern Catholic churches speak of themselves as a sign that East and West can share one communion. Some Orthodox see the Eastern Catholic churches differently, as a wound from the past. Catholic and Orthodox theologians have said together that bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today. Both views are held by people of good faith. Last, what's in reach now. Paul writes, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." Catholics and Orthodox can pray for each other, visit each other, learn each other's hymns, and greet each other at Pascha with the same words. The day of full communion isn't here. But the embrace came first, before any agreement, and the road starts there.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · `SO MUCH ALREADY SHARED.` · `THE HONEST PART: TWO VIEWS.` · `THE EMBRACE CAME FIRST.` · then, large: `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold East and West together. Settle, and breathe. On the in-breath, picture a Latin church you know: the altar, the pews, the crucifix. On the out-breath, picture one of the Eastern churches from these days: a wall of icons, a priest's family, a cedar, a candle passed hand to hand. Keep breathing between the two, letting neither crowd out the other. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own words, that they all may be one. If you don't, simply hold both pictures, side by side, and let them be at peace for a while. The bell holds the time.
Toward unity. The long work of Catholics and Orthodox to become one communion again, through prayer, dialogue and friendship, begun with an embrace. Today's word.

Your line: one day together. Today, make the first move toward someone you've drifted from. Not a treaty. Just the embrace. Tomorrow a new stretch begins: devotions. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church takes part in official theological dialogue with the Orthodox churches, and popes and patriarchs meet, pray together and exchange delegations on their churches' patronal feasts; Catholics pray for Christian unity, including during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

what a scholar hears: the mutual excommunications were lifted after a pope and an ecumenical patriarch met in Jerusalem; official dialogue continues, and Catholic and Orthodox theologians jointly rejected 'uniatism' as a method of unity today.

notes: Index hook: '1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025'. Script omits the number and year under the claims rule ('Catholics and Orthodox have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together'). Confirm, including Pope Leo XIV's visit to Nicaea (İznik) with Patriarch Bartholomew in late 2025 if the editor wants it named.

The Jerusalem embrace of Paul VI and Athenagoras (January 1964) and the lifting of the 1054 excommunications (December 1965) are told without names in the hook and without dates. Confirm 'afterward' sequencing and the kiss of peace detail.
'Their churches have been divided for centuries': confirm.
Balamand statement (1993) summarized as 'bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today'; confirm the paraphrase.
Orthodox view of Eastern Catholic churches 'as a wound from the past' and Eastern Catholic self-understanding presented side by side, unranked. Confirm fairness to both.
'Catholics and Orthodox share the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles' reflects Unitatis Redintegratio 15; confirm wording.
Douay-Rheims wording of John 17:21 and Ephesians 4:5: confirm.
End of the Eastern Catholic churches section (days 1357–1371); the carry points to the Devotions section starting day 1372.
